name: Mining Reward
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: The Carrot That Keeps Miners Honest: Understanding Mining Reward
lesson.summary: The mining reward is the payment, made up of newly issued tokens plus collected transaction fees, that compensates miners for the computational work of securing a proof of work blockchain, and its scheduled decline over time functions as the network's built in monetary policy.
lesson.body:
Mining, as covered earlier, is the process by which participants compete to solve a computationally difficult puzzle in order to win the right to add the next block to the chain. That competition only works because winning pays off, and the payment a miner receives for successfully mining a block is called the mining reward. It has two components: a block subsidy, which is a fixed amount of brand new tokens created by the protocol itself, and the sum of the transaction fees attached to every transaction the miner included in that block. Since this reward is paid in the network's own token, it directly ties the economics of mining to the value and issuance rules of that token.

Bitcoin is the clearest illustration of how this works. When Bitcoin launched in 2009, the block subsidy was fifty bitcoin per block. The protocol includes a rule that cuts this subsidy in half every 210,000 blocks, which works out to roughly every four years, an event known as the halving. The subsidy dropped to twenty five bitcoin in 2012, twelve and a half in 2016, six and a quarter in 2020, and three and one eighth in 2024. This geometric decline is what caps Bitcoin's total supply at twenty one million coins, with the final fractions of a coin not expected to be mined until around the year 2140.

The halving schedule is not just a technical curiosity, it is a deliberate monetary design choice. By steadily shrinking the rate of new token issuance, the protocol makes bitcoin progressively scarcer over time, similar in spirit to a central bank tapering the growth of a money supply, except the schedule is fixed in code rather than subject to a committee's discretion. As the block subsidy shrinks, transaction fees are intended to make up a larger share of what miners actually earn, a transition that has not fully played out yet but is built into the network's long term design.

Mining reward also functions as the network's security budget. Miners are rational economic actors, they invest in specialized hardware and pay for electricity because the expected reward, in tokens, multiplied by the token's market price, exceeds their costs. This means the reward has to stay high enough, relative to the cost of hashing power, to keep enough miners competing that no single actor could plausibly gather enough computing power to overwhelm the network. When token prices fall sharply or a halving cuts the subsidy, some miners whose costs are highest become unprofitable and shut down, an event sometimes referred to informally as miner capitulation, which temporarily lowers the network's total hash rate until the remaining miners' economics stabilize.

This dependence on continuous energy expenditure to fund security is precisely the feature that proof of stake, covered next, was designed to avoid. Rather than paying miners to burn electricity, proof of stake pays validators to lock up capital, replacing a physical cost with a financial one.
